title: mpCGCdb: polysaccharide-utilization gene clusters across the ocean
text:
The mpCGC pipeline




Figure 1. The three mpCGC dataflows: CGC annotation (orange), mining for networks and phylogenies (green), and summary and diversity statistics (blue).



Genes are predicted with Pyrodigal and annotated by DIAMOND and PyHMMER against dbCAN (CAZymes), SulfAtlas (sulfatases) and TCDB (transporters). A seed-and-extend algorithm then joins co-localized enzymes and transporters into clusters. The pipeline runs on conda, Docker, Singularity or Slurm, so the same workflow scaled to all 22,607 genomes. Its code is on GitHub.

title: mpCGCdb: polysaccharide-utilization gene clusters across the ocean
text:
Undiscovered cluster diversity




Figure 2. iNEXT rarefaction and extrapolation of CGC richness by lineage. Each genome is a sampling unit, and each CGC is encoded by the presence or absence of its CAZyme and sulfatase families. Solid lines show interpolation and dotted lines show extrapolation, with 95% bootstrap intervals.



Firmicutes, Bacteroidota and Planctomycetota hold the richest sets of cluster types, and Cyanobacteria, Desulfobacterota and Archaea the poorest. Chao2 estimates predict more than 9,000 distinct CAZyme and sulfatase arrangements in marine Bacteroidota and more than 4,000 in Planctomycetota. Current metagenomes capture under 40% of them.

title: mpCGCdb: polysaccharide-utilization gene clusters across the ocean
text:
Phylum-specific signatures




Figure 3. (A) UMAP of the CAZyme and sulfatase content of each genome’s CGCs, colored by phylum. (B) Share of each genome’s genes that fall inside CGCs.



Phylum explains about 12% of the variation in cluster composition (PERMANOVA pseudo-F = 169.8, p < 0.001), but the groups overlap rather than separate cleanly. Every major phylum includes genomes with a large share of their genes in CGCs: 1,070 genomes have more than 10%. Many are uncharacterized strains, such as Cohnella sp. CIP 111063 (24.3%) and Sedimentisphaera salicampi (19.3%), which are candidates for cultivation.

title: mpCGCdb: polysaccharide-utilization gene clusters across the ocean
text:
Enzyme colocalization




Figure 5. (A) How often each enzyme family (y) is found in a CGC that contains the anchor family (x), for families in at least 100 CGCs. (B to J) Blocks along the diagonal that correspond to substrate-specific modules.



Families that share a substrate cluster together. The blocks along the diagonal match α-glucan, β-glucan, alginate and glycosaminoglycan, mannan, pectin, arabinan, xylan and fucan pathways. Lineages specialize: Bacteroidota in α- and β-glucans, Verrucomicrobiota and Planctomycetota in sulfated fucans, and Firmicutes in pectin. Several sulfatase subfamilies with no assigned EC number appear in these modules. S1_23, S1_24 and S1_28 likely act on sulfated fucans, while S1_30 and S1_56 sit with laminarin and alginate enzymes. These associations suggest substrates for uncharacterized sulfatases.






TipMore data



mpcgcdb.com has a page for every enzyme family, lineage, genome and gene cluster, with a gene map for each cluster. Bulk annotations are on Zenodo, and the pipeline can be installed with nextflow run AaronAOliver/mpCGC.

title: Microbial guilds that detoxify and depolymerize seaweed
text:
Paper: Plominsky, Oliver et al. 2026, mBio Code: Enrichments_metatranscriptomics Data: MAGs on Zenodo SRA PRJNA1404287
Seaweed is hard to digest for two reasons. Its polysaccharides are diverse and sulfated, and it contains polyphenols (phlorotannins and their breakdown products) that inhibit microbial growth and enzymes. Hindgut contents from six Kyphosus cinerascens fish were used to start anaerobic in vitro microcosms fed different combinations of macroalgal and host-associated media. Four of these kept 96 to 99% of the active hindgut families. They were sampled on days 3, 8 and 16 for paired metagenomics and metatranscriptomics.
Mapping RNA reads back to MAGs shows which genome expresses which enzyme, and when. The early colonists detoxify polyphenols and degrade alginate. Later guilds take on the more recalcitrant sulfated polysaccharides.
This repository contains my part of the study: the genome-resolved expression analysis and the figures built from it.
Code
mag_info <- read.delim(ed("data", "microcosm_mag_info.txt"), check.names = FALSE) %>%
  filter(taxa != "Unclassified")
# one taxonomy per dereplicated population (bin_taxonomy.tab lists every member bin,
# and one population's members disagree, so it would double-count in a join)
parent_tax <- select(mag_info, parent_bin = bin, taxonomy = taxa)
map_rate <- read.delim(ed("data", "mapping_rate.tab"))

samples_ord <- c("FISH_1","FISH_2","FISH_3","FISH_4","FISH_5","FISH_6","T0_AVG",
                 "M30_T03","M30_T08","M30_T16","M36_T03","M36_T08","M36_T16",
                 "M75_T03","M75_T08","M75_T16","M78_T03","M78_T08","M78_T16")
sample_meta <- tibble(sample = samples_ord) %>%
  mutate(group = case_when(str_starts(sample, "FISH") ~ "Wild hindgut",
                           sample == "T0_AVG" ~ "Inoculum (T0)",
                           TRUE ~ str_extract(sample, "^M\\d+")),
         day = case_when(sample == "T0_AVG" ~ 0,
                         str_starts(sample, "M") ~ as.numeric(str_extract(sample, "\\d+$")),
                         TRUE ~ NA_real_))

                            "Desulfobacterota","Fusobacteriota","Gammaproteobacteria",

text:
1 Approach






flowchart LR
  F[6 hindguts] --> I[Pooled inoculum] --> M[4 microcosms<br/>days 3, 8, 16]
  M --> G[Metagenomes<br/>1,153 MAGs<br/>dRep: 471 populations]
  M --> T[Metatranscriptomes<br/>Bowtie2 + RSEM]
  G --> A[dbCAN, SulfAtlas,<br/>CAMPER]
  A --> N[TPM per gene, scaled<br/>by mapping rate]
  T --> N






All samples (fish, inoculum and microcosms) were sequenced for both metagenomes and metatranscriptomes.
Only 15 to 60% of reads in each sample map to the binned genomes. Raw TPMs are therefore scaled by each sample’s mapping rate, so that expression is comparable between samples with different binning coverage. This was the core normalization step in the original analysis:

# Scale RSEM TPMs by the fraction of reads that are MAG-resolved
rsem_norm <- rsem
for (samp in sample_list) {
  rate <- dplyr::filter(mapping_rate, sample == samp)$map_rate * 0.01
  rsem_norm[[samp]] <- rsem_norm[[samp]] * rate + 1e-8
}
# Collapse the four T0 replicates into a single inoculum profile
rsem_norm$T0_AVG <- rowMeans(rsem_norm[, c("T0_A", "T0_B", "T0_C", "T0_D")])



Code
map_rate %>%
  filter(sample %in% samples_ord | str_starts(sample, "T0")) %>%
  mutate(sample = factor(sample, levels = unique(c(samples_ord[1:6], sort(sample[str_starts(sample, "T0")]),
                                                   samples_ord[8:19])))) %>%
  mutate(Group = case_when(str_starts(sample, "FISH") ~ "Wild hindgut",
                           str_starts(sample, "T0") ~ "Inoculum (T0 replicates)",
                           TRUE ~ "Microcosm"),
         Group = factor(Group, levels = c("Wild hindgut", "Inoculum (T0 replicates)", "Microcosm"))) %>%
  plot_ly(x = ~sample, y = ~map_rate, color = ~Group, type = "bar",
          colors = c("Wild hindgut" = "#4ea3ff", "Inoculum (T0 replicates)" = "#9aa3b2", Microcosm = site_teal),
          hovertemplate = "%{x}: %{y:.1f}% of reads map to MAGs<extra></extra>") %>%
  layout(xaxis = list(title = "", tickangle = -45), yaxis = list(title = "% of reads mapped to MAGs", ticksuffix = "%"),
         legend = list(orientation = "h", y = 1.15)) %>%
  dark_layout()

The tree shows the dereplicated MAG populations. The rings give each genome’s count of red-algal CAZymes, brown-algal CAZymes, sulfatases and polyphenol-degrading genes. section: 3 Expression of CAZymes and sulfatases over time
text:
3 Expression of CAZymes and sulfatases over time
The plot below sums CAZyme and sulfatase TPM for each MAG population, grouped by phylum, and follows each microcosm from the inoculum to day 16. Choose a microcosm with the buttons.


Code
cs <- read.csv(ed("parent_bin_cazy_sulf.csv"), check.names = FALSE) %>%
  pivot_longer(-parent_bin, names_to = "sample", values_to = "tpm") %>%
  left_join(parent_tax, by = "parent_bin") %>%
  filter(!is.na(taxonomy), taxonomy != "Unclassified")

micro <- c("M30", "M36", "M75", "M78")
area <- map_dfr(micro, function(m) {
  cs %>% filter(sample == "T0_AVG" | str_starts(sample, m)) %>%
    mutate(microcosm = m, day = if_else(sample == "T0_AVG", 0, as.numeric(str_extract(sample, "\\d+$"))))
}) %>% group_by(microcosm, day, taxonomy) %>% summarise(tpm = sum(tpm), .groups = "drop")

taxa_present <- intersect(names(tax_cols_mt), unique(area$taxonomy))
fig <- plot_ly()
for (m in micro) for (tx in taxa_present) {
  d <- filter(area, microcosm == m, taxonomy == tx) %>% arrange(day)
  fig <- add_trace(fig, data = d, x = ~day, y = ~tpm, name = tx, type = "scatter", mode = "lines",
                   stackgroup = "one", line = list(width = .5, color = tax_cols_mt[[tx]]),
                   fillcolor = tax_cols_mt[[tx]], legendgroup = tx, showlegend = TRUE,
                   visible = m == micro[1],
                   hovertemplate = paste0(tx, "<br>day %{x}: %{y:,.0f} TPM<extra></extra>"))
}
nt <- length(taxa_present)
btns <- lapply(seq_along(micro), function(i)
  list(method = "update", label = micro[i],
       args = list(list(visible = rep(seq_along(micro) == i, each = nt)),
                   list(title = list(text = paste("Microcosm", micro[i]), font = list(size = 13), x = .99, xanchor = "right")))))
fig %>%
  layout(updatemenus = list(list(type = "buttons", direction = "right", buttons = btns,
                                 x = 0, y = 1.15, xanchor = "left", bgcolor = "#dfe5ec", bordercolor = "#8a93a3", font = list(color = "#111"))),
         title = list(text = "Microcosm M30", font = list(size = 13), x = .99, xanchor = "right"), margin = list(t = 70),
         xaxis = list(title = "Day", tickvals = c(0, 3, 8, 16), ticktext = c("T0", "3", "8", "16")),
         yaxis = list(title = "CAZyme + sulfatase TPM"),
         legend = list(title = list(text = "<b>Phylum</b>"))) %>%
  dark_layout()







3.1 Share of each genome’s transcription spent on these enzymes
For every MAG with at least 100 TPM in a sample, the plot shows the share of its expression that goes to CAZymes, sulfatases or detoxification genes. At their peak, individual Bacteroidota and Verrucomicrobiota MAGs put 5 to 7% of their transcription into sulfatases. One Bacillota MAG puts over 20% into detoxification genes.

  read.delim(ed("cazy_expression_short.tab")) %>% mutate(set = "CAZymes"),

) %>% filter(!is.na(taxonomy), taxonomy != "Unclassified") %>%

3.2 Genomic potential vs. realized expression
The x-axis is the fraction of the genome that encodes each enzyme class. The y-axis is the highest fraction of that MAG’s transcripts in any sample. Points near the dotted line express an enzyme class in proportion to its gene count.

mp <- read.delim(ed("max_pct_1k.tab"), check.names = FALSE) %>% rename(taxonomy = `taxonomic group`) %>%
  filter(taxonomy != "Unclassified")
pairs <- list(CAZymes = c("pct_cazy_genome", "max_cazy_pct"),
              Sulfatases = c("pct_sulf_genome", "max_sulf_pct"),
              Detoxification = c("pct_detox_genome", "max_detox_pct"))
fig <- plot_ly()
for (s in names(pairs)) {
  d <- mp %>% transmute(bin, taxonomy, x = .data[[pairs[[s]][1]]], y = .data[[pairs[[s]][2]]]) %>%
    filter(!is.na(y))
  fig <- add_trace(fig, data = d, x = ~x, y = ~y, color = ~taxonomy, colors = tax_cols_mt,
                   type = "scatter", mode = "markers", visible = s == "CAZymes",
                   legendgroup = ~taxonomy, showlegend = TRUE,
                   marker = list(size = 8, opacity = .8, line = list(width = .4, color = "#111")),
                   text = ~paste0("<b>", bin, "</b><br>", taxonomy), hoverinfo = "text+x+y")
}

# CAZymes span up to ~20%; sulfatases and detoxification stay under 5%, so zoom those panels to 0-5%

  } else {

  }
  list(method = "update", label = names(pairs)[i],
       args = list(list(visible = rep(seq_along(pairs) == i, each = ntx)), lay))
})

  layout(updatemenus = list(list(type = "buttons", direction = "right", buttons = btns, x = 0, y = 1.15,
                                 xanchor = "left", bgcolor = "#dfe5ec", bordercolor = "#8a93a3", font = list(color = "#111"))),

title: Microbial guilds that detoxify and depolymerize seaweed
text:
5 Takeaways

Kept in vitro, the hindgut microbiome reproduces a staged breakdown of seaweed. Gammaproteobacteria detoxify polyphenols and degrade alginate first. Bacillota, Bacteroidota and Verrucomicrobiota guilds then attack the sulfated polysaccharides.
Sulfatase-rich Bacteroidota and Verrucomicrobiota MAGs put up to 5 to 7% of their transcription into sulfatases at their peak.
These microcosms are a tractable model for discovering CAZymes and marine polyphenol-degradation pathways.







NoteReproducing this page





The figures here use the processed summary tables in the repository: per-MAG expression shares, MAG metadata, and the dereplicated MAG tree stored in .RData. The full RSEM gene-by-sample matrix (data/binned_expression_fixed.tab), which genome_resolved_expression.R reads, is not in the repository. The enzyme-level panels are therefore shown as the published figures rather than recomputed here.

Paper: Oliver et al. 2024, mBio Code: KyphosusMAGs Data: MAGs on Zenodo SRA PRJNA819194 / PRJNA1023379
Herbivorous Kyphosus fish (nenue, or rudderfish) live on red, green and brown seaweed and rely on gut microbes to break down its polysaccharides. Algal glycans such as agar, carrageenan, alginate, fucoidan and ulvan are heavily sulfated, so the industrial enzymes used for land plants work poorly on them. We recovered metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from wild fish guts and from bioreactors seeded with gut contents, and identified which microbes carry the enzymes for each step of degradation.
This notebook rebuilds the main analyses from the processed tables in the repository. Most figures are interactive: hover for values, click legend entries to hide groups, and drag to zoom.

4 Short-chain fatty acid production
The fish get much of their energy from short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) made by fermentation. gutSMASH was used to find the pathways for each SCFA. Bubble size is the percentage of MAGs in a lineage that carry the pathway.

scfa <- read.delim(kd("scfa_breakdown.tab"), check.names = FALSE) %>%
  pivot_longer(-Taxa, names_to = "Pathway", values_to = "Fraction") %>%
  mutate(Pathway = str_trim(Pathway),

text:
5 Similarity to reference enzymes
Each binned CAZyme and sulfatase was compared against three references: other MAGs in this study, GenBank nr, and the curated CAZy or SulfAtlas databases. Across all annotated genes, the median best-hit identity is 63% to GenBank nr, 56% to CAZy and 36% to SulfAtlas. Most are distant from characterized enzymes, so the Kyphosus gut is a likely source of new seaweed-degrading enzymes.
The plot shows the five CAZyme and five sulfatase families (from the algal-polysaccharide families analyzed in the paper) whose genes are least similar to anything in GenBank nr. Their median best-hit identity is about 40 to 60%.

  mutate(across(c(nr_id, self_id, sulf_id, dbCAN_id), ~ suppressWarnings(as.numeric(.x))))

               "S1_15","S1_16","S1_17","S1_28","S1_25","S1_14","S1_27")

# the 5 families per class with the lowest median identity to GenBank nr
least_similar <- function(fams) {
  nov %>% filter(annot %in% fams) %>% group_by(annot) %>%
    summarise(med = median(nr_id, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% slice_min(med, n = 5) %>% pull(annot)
}
cz <- least_similar(cazy_fams); sf <- least_similar(sulf_fams)

6 A GH86 β-agarase/β-porphyranase with an undescribed domain
GH86 enzymes cut agar and porphyran, the main glycans of red algae. The gene tree of binned GH86 sequences has a clade from three different phyla (Bacillota, Bacteroidota and Verrucomicrobiota) that share an N-terminal region with no characterized function. Most of these sequences also have a signal peptide, so they are likely exported. This is consistent with several taxa breaking these glycans down outside the cell.

text:
8 Takeaways

Bacteroidota MAGs carry the widest range of algal-polysaccharide enzymes, but few single genomes can fully break down any one sulfated algal glycan.
The enzymes needed are split across lineages, and many have signal peptides, suggesting that Kyphosus symbionts degrade seaweed jointly, outside the cell.
Many of the CAZymes, sulfatases and BGCs are distant from characterized references, so these bioreactor communities are a source of new enzymes.

text:
How a SCoNe is built






flowchart TB
  P[Proteins<br/>all-vs-all DIAMOND] --> S[Sequence similarity<br/>network]
  S --> L[Weighted Leiden<br/>homology communities]
  N[Gene neighborhoods<br/>dbCAN CGCs, antiSMASH BGCs<br/>Spacedust synteny, flanking genes] --> C
  L --> C[Count community pairs<br/>that share a neighborhood]
  C --> X[SCoNe<br/>nodes = communities<br/>edges = conserved colocalization]






The tool reads the neighborhoods as input rather than inferring them. The same code can therefore work on dbCAN gene clusters, antiSMASH regions, Spacedust synteny blocks, or the genes around one query gene.

Step 1: a sequence similarity network
The synthetic dataset from Figure 2.1 has 712 proteins from 30 planted families, spread across 22 gene clusters. All-vs-all DIAMOND hits with an E-value of 10-10 or lower are kept, and each edge is weighted by -log10(E-value), as in build_ssn_leiden.py.

mock = REPO / "examples" / "mock"
cols = ["q", "s", "pident", "len", "mm", "gap", "qs", "qe", "ss", "se", "evalue", "bits"]
hits = pd.read_csv(mock / "diamond.tsv", sep="\t", names=cols)
hits = hits[(hits.q != hits.s) & (hits.evalue <= 1e-10)].copy()
hits["a"] = hits[["q", "s"]].min(axis=1)
hits["b"] = hits[["q", "s"]].max(axis=1)
edges = (hits.groupby(["a", "b"], as_index=False)["evalue"].min()
             .assign(weight=lambda d: -np.log10(d.evalue.clip(lower=1e-300))))

nodes = pd.read_csv(mock / "nodes.txt", header=None)[0].tolist()
truth = pd.read_csv(mock / "annotations.tsv", sep="\t").set_index("protein_id")["gene"]

g = ig.Graph()
g.add_vertices(nodes)
g.add_edges(list(zip(edges.a, edges.b)))
g.es["weight"] = edges.weight.tolist()
print(f"{g.vcount()} proteins, {g.ecount():,} similarity edges")

712 proteins, 10,645 similarity edges




Step 2: homology communities with weighted Leiden

part = g.community_leiden(objective_function="modularity", weights="weight",
                          resolution=1.0, n_iterations=-1)
leiden = dict(zip(nodes, part.membership))
fam = [truth.get(n, "none") for n in nodes]
print(f"{len(part)} Leiden communities; "
      f"ARI vs. planted families = {ari(part.membership, fam):.3f}")

30 Leiden communities; ARI vs. planted families = 0.907



layout = g.layout_fruchterman_reingold(weights=[np.log1p(w) for w in g.es["weight"]], niter=500, seed=None)
xy = np.array(layout.coords)
ex, ey = [], []
for e in g.es.select(lambda e: e.index % 3 == 0):         # draw every third edge to keep the figure light
    s, t = e.tuple
    ex += [xy[s, 0], xy[t, 0], None]; ey += [xy[s, 1], xy[t, 1], None]
palette = px.colors.qualitative.Dark24 + px.colors.qualitative.Light24
fig = go.Figure()
fig.add_trace(go.Scattergl(x=ex, y=ey, mode="lines", line=dict(width=.4, color="#5a6272"),
                           hoverinfo="skip", showlegend=False))
fig.add_trace(go.Scattergl(
    x=xy[:, 0], y=xy[:, 1], mode="markers",
    marker=dict(size=8, color=[palette[m % len(palette)] for m in part.membership],
                line=dict(width=.3, color="#111")),
    text=[f"{n}<br>planted family: {f}<br>Leiden community {m}" for n, f, m in zip(nodes, fam, part.membership)],
    hoverinfo="text", showlegend=False))
fig.update_layout(height=430, margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=10, b=10),
                  xaxis=dict(visible=False), yaxis=dict(visible=False))
show(fig)

                            
                                            
The mock SSN colored by Leiden community. Hover over a node to see its planted family. Some families split into several communities, which the SCoNe step then handles.




Step 3: collapse communities and add colocalization edges
Each gene cluster adds 1 to the weight of every pair of communities it contains, counted once per neighborhood. Edge weight is therefore the number of independent neighborhoods in which two homology groups appear together.

cmap = pd.read_csv(mock / "cluster_genome_map.tsv", sep="\t")
comm_size = collections.Counter(part.membership)
co = collections.Counter()
for genes in cmap.genes:
    comms = sorted({leiden[x] for x in genes.split(",") if x in leiden})
    co.update(itertools.combinations(comms, 2))

# label each community by its majority planted family (>= 75%), else auxiliary_N
labels = {}
for c in comm_size:
    members = [truth.get(n, "none") for n in nodes if leiden[n] == c]
    top, k = collections.Counter(members).most_common(1)[0]
    labels[c] = top if k / len(members) >= .75 else f"auxiliary_{c}"

sc = ig.Graph()
sc.add_vertices(sorted(comm_size))
sc.add_edges([(a, b) for a, b in co])
sc.es["weight"] = list(co.values())
print(f"SCoNe: {sc.vcount()} community nodes, {sc.ecount()} colocalization edges "
      f"(max weight {max(co.values())})")

SCoNe: 30 community nodes, 160 colocalization edges (max weight 8)



pos = np.array(sc.layout_kamada_kawai().coords)   # spreads the dense block more evenly than FR
fig = go.Figure()
wmax = max(sc.es["weight"])
for e in sc.es:
    s, t = e.tuple; w = e["weight"]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[pos[s, 0], pos[t, 0]], y=[pos[s, 1], pos[t, 1]], mode="lines",
                             line=dict(width=.5 + 5 * w / wmax, color=f"rgba(140,210,213,{.15 + .75 * w / wmax:.2f})"),
                             hoverinfo="text", text=f"{labels[s]} and {labels[t]}: {w} clusters", showlegend=False))
vids = list(range(sc.vcount()))
fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
    x=pos[:, 0], y=pos[:, 1], mode="markers+text",
    marker=dict(size=[(12 + 5.25 * np.sqrt(comm_size[v])) / 1.6 for v in vids],
                color=[palette[v % len(palette)] for v in vids], line=dict(width=1, color="#111")),
    text=[labels[v] for v in vids], textposition="top center", textfont=dict(size=10, color="#eaeaea"),
    hovertext=[f"<b>{labels[v]}</b><br>{comm_size[v]} proteins<br>degree {sc.degree(v)}" for v in vids],
    hoverinfo="text", showlegend=False))
fig.update_layout(height=480, margin=dict(l=10, r=10, t=10, b=10),
                  xaxis=dict(visible=False), yaxis=dict(visible=False))
show(fig)

                            
                                            
The mock SCoNe. Node size follows community size (12 + 5.25 times the square root of n, as in the tool). Edge width and opacity follow how many gene clusters share the pair. Hover over a node to see its family.




Scoring a SCoNe
scone_metrics.py defines SCoNe Edge Agreement (SEA). It is an adjusted Rand index computed over the colocalization edges rather than over genes, so it only penalizes partition differences that change the network’s wiring. The package also defines colocalization modularity, which measures how well a partition lines up communities with the block structure of the neighborhoods.

coloc_edges = set()
for genes in cmap.genes:
    coloc_edges.update(itertools.combinations(sorted(x for x in genes.split(",") if x), 2))
p_leiden = {n: str(leiden[n]) for n in nodes}
p_truth = {n: truth.get(n, "none") for n in nodes}
p_singletons = {n: n for n in nodes}
pd.DataFrame({
    "Partition": ["Weighted Leiden", "Planted families", "Every protein alone"],
    "SEA vs. planted": [sea(coloc_edges, p_leiden, p_truth), 1.0, sea(coloc_edges, p_singletons, p_truth)],
    "Colocalization modularity": [coloc_modularity(coloc_edges, p) for p in (p_leiden, p_truth, p_singletons)],
}).style.hide(axis="index").format(precision=3)

Across genomes, CAZyme and sulfatase counts are only weakly correlated (Spearman’s rho = 0.18).
